utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration. If you would stand up, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd care to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Alex Whiting for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, could you please state your name.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Vlado Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, on June 18th of this year, did you have occasion to go over your witness statement in the presence of an officer of the court and attest to its accuracy, and did you sign a declaration attesting to its accuracy?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would offer the statement of Mr. Vukovic into evidence pursuant to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Prosecution Exhibit 479.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got a copy of that package?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We received it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would read a copy of the statement. I would first draw the Court's attention to page 19 of the atlas, in particular the lower section grid reference D-E 2 and 3, and the villages that the witness will be speaking about are located in that part of page 19. The witness is a Croat who was 29 years old at the time of the events. He joined the police force in December of 1990 and was first assigned to Ogulin. He was transferred to Saborsko on the 1st of April, 1991. In the month of April, 1991, in the neighbouring Serb village of Plaski, there was a protest in which the inhabitants demanded an ethnically pure Serb police. In June of 1991, the Serb police officers changed the patches on their uniforms to militia Krajina patches. In the same time period, Martic's Police appeared in the area. Civilians could only travel in the area by buses which were routinely stopped and searched by Martic's militia. The police in Saborsko were not allowed to travel outside of the village at this time. On August 5th of 1991, the shelling of Saborsko began from the direction of Licka Jesenica, a Serb area. That evening, some police officers from Duga Rese who had come before the attack to help the local police left Saborsko with a number of elderly women and children. From that day on, Serb forces shelled Saborsko nearly every day, sometimes using cluster bombs and destroying many houses. The witness and two other police officers were captured on September 29th, 1991, by members of Martic's police. They were taken first to the gaol in Plaski where the witness was kept for 12 days and beaten several times by Martic's Police. Then he was transferred to the prison in Korenica where he was also severely beaten. His teeth were knocked out and he was locked in solitary confinement. After approximately 12 days, he and other prisoners were taken by the JNA to Zeljava airport near Bihac where he was held for more than five days. There he was beaten by JNA military police. He was told that the men beating him were former Serb police colleagues from Zagreb. The witness was taken to Manjaca camp near Banja Luka and on November 9, 1991, he was exchanged with about 200 other prisoners for Serb JNA officers and soldiers. On about August 7, 1995, shortly after Operation Storm, he returned to Saborsko. He could not recognise his village as everything was overgrown and abandoned. In that month of August, the witness attended two exhumations in Saborsko. In addition, ten skeletons of elderly people were found in their homes. They had either been killed and burnt with their homes or killed when their homes were burned. In all, 29 to 30 bodies were found and seven villagers are still missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a few additional questions related to tab 2 of Exhibit 479.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If that could be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is, rather, an annex of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, could you look at the names on that list that has been set before you. Do you recognise those names?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 90 per cent of them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are those former residents of Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your knowledge, were the people on those -- on that list combatants or civilians?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: All of them were civilians except Mate Spehar who was a Croatian policeman, on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In your statement you refer to an exhumation where the body of a policeman was found in a grave. Is that the body of this individual?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a mass gravesite, Popov Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, my last question is: Do you know anything about the ages of the people on this list in general?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were all people who were roughly about 60 to 70 years of age, women too, and men, and there was one person who was older, Mate Matovina. He was born in 18-something. It says 95 here. He was one of the oldest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukovic, you said that your previous profession was policeman; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 2 of your statement, it says that from the moment you did your military service in the JNA up to 1989, you worked on the construction of prefabricated houses throughout Yugoslavia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that from November 1989 to the 15th of December 1990 you were unemployed, in fact?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you attend a training course for policemen or did you join the MUP without having had any previous training, the MUP of the Republic of Croatia, that is.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I did attend a course for policemen once I passed my medical examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That was in 1990. When I enrolled, I went. After I had enrolled, I went to attend this education course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And in paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that you and four other colleagues of yours at Plitvice Jezera, the lakes of Plitvice, tendered in your resignation because the Serbs were in the majority there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true and correct that in that same paragraph you said that the Serbs were in the majority in this area and even though there was nothing happening in particular, nothing concrete happened, we just felt uneasy and decided to leave and find work elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you feel uneasy somewhere and undesirable, where Serb songs are being sung, where people joke and -- don't joke but say quite seriously some things, why would you be in company of that kind? It's better to leave and then not have any problems. I wasn't the only one who left; a number of us left. And actually, that's what happened later on. The Croats left the Plitvice Lakes area en masse who had had jobs there. Those of them who stayed on suffered the fate that happened to them in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you left because you didn't like the presence of Serbs. You said that nothing actually happened.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it didn't. Now, why, if I have an option? I worked in the forestry department for a time, so that was another option.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3, you say that you could feel things were changing, however, there was nothing particular going on in Saborsko. That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Has the witness a copy of his statement? He does. Yes. Repeat the question, if you would, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in paragraph 3, you say that you could feel things were changing, however, there was nothing particular happening in Saborsko. And that's what you say. I have your statement in front of me. It reads as follows: "We could feel things were changing. However, there was nothing particularly happening in Saborsko. We could all still move around freely, and the Serbs still came to our village."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the question is: How was the situation changing if nothing was actually happening in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was referring to 1990, because in 1990 you could still travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vukovic. Now, is it true that in 1990, of the 800 inhabitants of Saborsko, there were only 15 Serbs, in fact?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why I wanted you to explain to me how you felt that the situation was changing in Saborsko in which the Serbs represented just a little over 1 per cent of the population? Or more exactly, if there were 15 Serbs of 855 inhabitants, that's 1.8 per cent.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm not quite clear on what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The question that he's asking is this: We're dealing with 1990, in the village, and you say, "We could feel things were changing," but you say nothing particular was happening in the village. Now, the question that he's asking is in what way could you feel things were changing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, things were changing in other parts of Croatia, but at that time in Saborsko, nothing had happened yet. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the next paragraph, paragraph 4, you say that with the Serbs in Saborsko, there was never -- there were never any problems. There were no problems. You say: "There were no problems with the Serbs in Saborsko." That's how you put it in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the three or four houses that were in Saborsko, those people were with us up to the fall of Saborsko itself. They were together with us. And we didn't have any problems with them, neither did they have any problems with us. We were together during the war, and they were my neighbours. I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were together during the war.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, until the fall of Saborsko on the 12th of November. They lived in Saborsko. They lived together with all the rest of the inhabitants of Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm not quite clear about your explanations as to why you left your job, because you say the situation was changing, and the situation changing in Saborsko, whereas in the place itself there were just 15 Serbs living there who didn't make any problems for you.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are mixing up Saborsko and Plitvice. They are two different concepts. Saborsko is one place; Plitvice is another. What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And when you spoke about the Plitvice Lakes, you said that nothing specific happened there. So was it prejudice on your side and a negative attitude towards the Serbs that prompted you or something else? Because at Plitvice you said nothing specific happened, and in Saborsko you lived together and, once again, there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't wish to answer questions of that type from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. You must -- look, I know he's asking the questions, but you're giving evidence to the Court, so could you remember that and don't be provoked by him. Just try and answer as best you can any questions he asks. Yes. I think you said earlier that there was -- that there was an unpleasant atmosphere, that sort of thing, is that right, which made you leave your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was at Plitvice Lakes and not in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I hope that neither of my questions can be described as being provocative. I'm just trying to establish what it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If they had been, you would have been stopped, but it may be the witness felt provoked. Yes. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vukovic, also in paragraph 4 you say that the Serbs stopped coming to Saborsko after the May referendum in 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Milosevic. Where did you read that from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The sentence reads: "We noticed that a number of the Serbs from other villages did not come to Saborsko any longer after the referendum in May 1990."

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Some Serbs, a certain number of Serbs, not all of them. Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that the question of the referendum was the independence of Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the referendum had been organised by the HDZ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes. There was the HDZ at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember, as you were a policeman and you knew, therefore -- you were familiar with the basic elements of the system, is it also true that the programme of the HDZ, according to its constitutional provisions, envisaged Croatia as a state of the Croats, depriving the Serbs of constituent rights?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to enter into a political debate now. We can address that elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it strange, then, that the Serbs didn't wish to come to Saborsko any longer?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs did come to Saborsko, Mr. Milosevic. Don't put all the Serbs in one group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not. I'm just referring to what you say.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was saying that some Serbs didn't come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vukovic. I was just quoting from your statement, but I don't wish to insist on that point any further. In paragraph 6 in your statement, you say that on the 1st of April, 1991, you were moved from the Ogulin SUP to Saborsko; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were transferred by the MUP of Croatia that you were employed in. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also go on to say that some policemen from Plasko that same month moved from Saborsko as well. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they also Croats?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: In the MUP of Croatia, both Croats and Serbs were employed, Mr. Milosevic. In the Plaski police station, there were Croats and Serbs working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about those who were transferred to Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were Croats, because they were no longer welcome over there. As you yourself know, the revolts had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Croats from Plasko were transferred to Saborsko, the policemen.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were transferred there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did they make such a request to be transferred to this other place or was this a decision taken by superior bodies?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Some Serbs in Plasko did not consider them to be welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this the same kind of situation as you had concluded that you were not welcome at Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. A rally, protests were being held. The Republic of Serbian Krajina was already slowly coming into being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Serb policemen in Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We collaborated in Saborsko and in Plaski with policemen of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what happened to the Serb policemen who, like you, no longer wanted to work with Croat policemen?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Serb policemen did work with Croat policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about those who did work. I'm asking you about those who did not wish to work with Croat policemen. Did the Croatian MUP transfer them to predominantly Serb villages or were they fired?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So no one transferred them?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbs from Croatia, copying the example of the Croats, also held a referendum at which they declared themselves in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that before the new constitution the Serbs were a constituent nation, and being that, they were entitled to a referendum?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Of course the Serbs are a constituent people in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that right was abolished with the new constitution. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But tell me, please, in paragraph 7 of your statement, you say that in Saborsko, up until the 4th of August, 1991, nothing happened. But you knew that people were getting killed in other villages in Croatia. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who were the conflicting parties?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The rebellious Serbs that did not wish to recognise the Republic of Croatia and that wanted to form the Republic of Serbian Krajina and which they were already forming.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean among them only or between them and somebody else?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not going to debate these political issues, not with this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness, Mr. May, in view of what he said in his statement in paragraph 7, that he knew that people were getting killed in other villages. So I asked him, since he speaks about that, who was fighting who, what kind of conflicts were going on, whether he knew anything about that, because that's what he mentions in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He mentioned that he heard about people being killed. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Had you heard of cases of killed Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that same paragraph, you say that at 6:00 a.m. on the 5th of August 1991, the first mortar rounds were fired at Saborsko, and this attack lasted until 10.00. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And already in the next sentence you say that prior to this attack another 20 police officers had come to Saborsko from Duga Rese as some sort of reinforcement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what came first, the attack on Saborsko or the arrival of these additional policemen?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the attack had been envisaged. We received anonymous information by phone to take care because we were surrounded because our roads were blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is Saborsko on a road between Knin and Slunj? Is it one of the major communication routes in that area?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not between Knin and Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, where is it, then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is between Plasko, Plitvice, and Korenica. Slunj is on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So is Saborsko on this main road, as you say?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Saborsko is on the road between Plitvice and Plasko.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So traffic had been interrupted there?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as I asked you a question about these police reinforcements, had they come before that attack on Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, even before, there had been provocations, before the shells started falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they arrived before the attack?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the shelling on the 5th of August went on for all of four hours. That's what you stated, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, there were no casualties, nor was a single house damaged. Is that what you've said?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, 80 shells fell on Saborsko of 82 millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But did you say that no damage was caused to buildings?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Up until 10.00, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What were the attackers on Saborsko targeting then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Ask them. I suppose they didn't have a proper orientation. But they did in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that 80 shells fell.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In Saborsko, on the 5th of August, 1991, were there any conflicts, an exchange of fire, or did the Serbs simply shell the place with mortar fire?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Without any cause, they simply shelled the village, and the locals of Licka Jesenica protested against this. We have evidence of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since the people of Licka Jesenica protested, I'm asking you whether there was an exchange of fire between your forces and the Serbs that were shelling Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Only occasionally they would use sniper fire, but people were working in the fields, and they would use snipers. But on the 5th of August, there was an open attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about that attack. So when that conflict broke out, was there an exchange of fire between both sides?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What did we have to respond with, rifles? We didn't have any mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't fire.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were armed. There were even reinforcements that had arrived, as we have established.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, a policeman doesn't have a mortar, a cannon, a tank. A policeman has his personal weapons; a rifle and a pistol. They didn't come to wage war up there, they came to preserve public law and order and the state of security. Who knew that there would be an open attack on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is the short answer, though, that there was no fire back from the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Serbs take control of Saborsko then?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They were shelling from a distance of 2 or 3 kilometres. They didn't come with the infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Is it true, Mr. Vukovic, that in the immediate vicinity of Saborsko, in Licka Jesenica, there was a large ammunition depot holding also fuel of the JNA? I assume, as a policeman, you must have known that.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Croatian armed units were trying for several months to take control of this depot and take over large quantities of ammunition, explosives, and fuel?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And what could they do that with?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether that is true, that Croatian armed formations had for several months been trying to take control of this warehouse. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And is it true that units of the JNA had tried to approach the warehouse from the direction of Saborsko and the soldiers in it, in the warehouse, and thereby to deblock that warehouse, because there were very few soldiers there guarding the warehouse, virtually just a group of soldiers, guards guarding the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: And who had blocked the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to information that I have, Mr. Vukovic, the warehouse had been blocked by armed Croatian forces, and they were trying to deblock this small group of soldiers. My question to you is whether you know that and whether that is true. You can just say yes or no. If you feel it's not true, say so and we can move on, because there's information about that.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that has nothing to do with reality, what you're saying, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's what he said. But you said the JNA had this depot. Were the JNA guarding it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't know about that. That was under the jurisdiction of the Republic of Srpska Krajina already. We had no idea about that. It was not under our control. It was held by the Martic men and the JNA. It was not under our control at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on the 23rd of September, 1991, a hundred or so men from Saborsko and the environs returned wearing uniforms of the National Guards Corps so as to prevent attempts by the JNA to deblock the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I understand.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Your question has -- has nothing to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I asked you whether it was true that about a hundred men returned. As you say this has nothing to do with anything, have a look at paragraph 9, if you would, and it says: "On the 23rd of September, a group of 100 men who had lived in Saborsko, natives of Saborsko, came back to the village to help defend it. These men wore the uniforms of a reserve police officer. Later on, this group of men was called the Independent Company of Saborsko. This was much needed help as the police were worn out. Once they arrived, they were divided into groups," and so on and so forth. So is it true that this particular unit, the one that came - and according to you, I know nothing about anything - I'm quoting from your statement where it says that that unit was later on called the Independent Company of Saborsko. That's what you wrote yourself in your statement.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as of the 5th of August to the 23rd of September, these policemen from Duga Rese that you mentioned left the same day, because you can't fight, you couldn't find up there. And we stayed alone. And in Saborsko, there was daily 100 to 200 shells being thrown on it up until the 23rd of September. And we asked for aid and assistance because we were left on our own, and they kept shelling. The 122-millimetre shells were used, as far as I know. And later on, God knows what else was used. That's where the problem lies, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you didn't explain this to me. You said they came and left and then you later on said that that particular group was -- came to be known as the Independent Company of Saborsko. Later on. That means later on it was proclaimed to be the Independent Company of Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That group arrived. From the reserve police force of Zagreb. They were locals, local people who had come back to defend the village of Saborsko, because there were so many shells falling on it from one day to the next, from one night to the next; that's where the problem lay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, I'm just trying to establish the facts on the basis of what you yourself say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got the statement. Now, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Vukovic, is it true that among the ranks of the Croatian forces there were a number of mercenaries fighting together with them in this attempt at the depot at Licka Jesenica?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're talking about. Who jeopardised those reserves? It was the JNA and the Martic men who were together, and until the 5th of August it passed through Saborsko's buffer zone. And what's the buffer zone? We know now what they did; they collaborated. There was no difference between the so-called Martic men and the JNA. Had there not been the JNA, there wouldn't have been any shelling of Saborsko either. Where would they have shelled it from? You mean the Martic men made grenades and shells overnight and the tanks and the armoured APC things they had?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, there was a large depot of the JNA in Licka Jesenica, no Martic police as you refer to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given -- just a moment. He's just given his evidence, and there's no use arguing with him about it, so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vukovic. In paragraph 10, you claim that on the 29th of September, 1991, you and two other colleagues of yours were captured by members of -- these people that you've referred to as Martic's Police or Martic's militia.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was in fact the police force of Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the police, it was the militia. Milicija. The police was what existed before the Republika Srpska Krajina, as it was called, was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was a police in Croatia and a police in the Republic of Srpska Krajina. It was no police force of Martic's. Not his personal police force, it was the police force of the Republika Srpska Krajina. Isn't that right, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I had a chance to see them when I was captured. I saw them myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vukovic. Now, tell me why you were captured. What was the reason?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I could ask you that, why I was captured, why I was arrested. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time you were arrested, were you wearing a uniform and the others who were with you too and arrested with you? You say that two other colleagues of yours were also taken captive on that occasion. Were you wearing uniforms or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We were wearing uniforms of the Croatian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what weapons did you have on you?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We had short-barrelled weapons and long-barrelled weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were armed and in uniform.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And what did you have in your car as you weren't driving an official vehicle?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, we didn't -- we couldn't drive an official vehicle. Why? Because the policemen used -- in official cars were targets of attacks. So we avoided using the official cars. I went to fetch food, and we avoided using official vehicles at all because there was shooting coming at us from all sides when people saw a police vehicle. We were in an encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And was anybody killed when there was this shooting from all sides, as you say?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Who wasn't killed is more to the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, give me a name. Did you see anybody killed when you were shot at from all sides?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't shot at. I didn't offer any resistance when they were capturing me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in the car, apart from the fact that you say that you had short and long-barrelled weapons, did you have any explosive devices at all?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: What are you talking about, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you. I'm asking you a short and clear question, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: We only had personal weapons on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Automatic weapons and pistols?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: An automatic rifle and a pistol, that's all, because we were moving towards the military training ground, and we were on -- in an encirclement. It was the Tobolic JNA training ground that was in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you whether anybody ever arrested you from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA and the Martic men, it's the same thing. The ones that captured me were wearing JNA soldiers. But whether they were JNA/Martic, it's all the same to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the fact that it's all the same to you, let's leave that to one side. But you were arrested by the police of Krajina, not the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: The six or seven of them were wearing JNA uniforms. Now, who they were, was he a JNA person or a Martic man, I don't know. In Plaski, I saw that that was all the same in Plaski when they arrested me. There was no difference. They were sleeping together, drinking together, walking around together. We all knew that. I know the people from Plaski by sight. One of them would wear a JNA uniform, the other would wear a camouflage uniform. Where's the difference? I don't see it. Both of them are camouflage uniforms and I'm a Martic man and he's a JNA man. What does that mean? Explain it to me. They were there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I understood from your statement that you were arrested by the police of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's how they introduced themselves, but it was the JNA uniform that they were wearing. This man was wearing a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. A JNA uniform was something that practically all the territorials wore and had, not only in Croatia but throughout Yugoslavia; isn't that right, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in paragraph 11, you say that when you were exchanged for JNA soldiers and officers, that you learnt that 10 of your colleagues had been killed in Saborsko, that ten of your policemen were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. killed in Saborsko. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I got to know about that after I had been captured and released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were they killed in conflicts with members of the JNA who held the blockade or were they killed in a clash with the police of Krajina? How were they killed?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know between which parties the clash took place. Now, who hit Saborsko, planes, mortars, the JNA, I keep repeating the same thing: The JNA and Martic's men, it's the same thing. Who armed the Serbs in Plaski? And people talk about this quite openly now. So what is it that you're talking about? And time has denied what you're saying. Had there not been the JNA, there wouldn't have been the Republika Srpska Krajina. People talk about that quite openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Today, people who live in the area refute what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you. I'm asking you questions normally.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking illogical questions. Well, times now have shown you to be wrong. The people are there. They were tricked. They recognise this themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you questions exclusively on the basis of what you say in your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've had sufficient of this argument. Now, have you got anything more you want to ask him about the statement, in particular the last paragraph about the exhumations? If you challenge any of that, you should ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand that, Mr. May, and that is precisely what I'm doing. And my questions -- it's not my questions that are making the witness nervous, it's something else, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I can see in paragraph 12 of your statement that you took an active part in Operation Storm; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Actively. What do you mean? We were the police force with the others. It was the Croatian army that came first. They were the forefront of the forces in the operation. We came second. The police was the force there to see to law and order and ensure that people were safe and secure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And you returned to Saborsko after that, where your task, as you yourself say, was to prevent retaliation and revenge actions, as you put it in your statement.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we managed to do that. After the evil and tragedy, this was not followed by another tragedy, and that is a good thing. And that is why people can live in the area now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me how many Serbs of those 15 have stayed on in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serbs stayed in Saborsko, and they're still living there today. They returned, and they stayed on after 1991. They just went to Licka Jesenica because they didn't want to continue living without us Croats, those three households, Serb households.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you say that you did not wish to allow any actions of retaliation and revenge to take place, do you have in mind when you say that just the situation in Saborsko where there were no Serbs or do you mean the attacks on the columns of Serb refugees during the exodus that took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, wait a moment. The witness can give evidence about what he saw and did, and he's told you. Now, are you suggesting that he attacked the column of refugees? If so, you must put it. Otherwise, it's not a proper question for him to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll ask Mr. Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you take part in the attacks on the columns of Serb refugees during that exodus from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. And in actual fact, there were no attacks of that kind. I don't know about them. In the area where I was and where we worked, there were no such attacks. As to other attacks, I don't know about them. I can't talk about things I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vukovic, fine. In the last paragraph of your statement, you speak about the exhumations that were carried out in the Saborsko area; right? Now, tell me, how many bodies were uncovered and exhumed later on?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of October, 1995, the exhumation process began, and at the time, 35 bodies were found after several days of exhumation. 20 something and then individual bodies, not all together. Some of them were in the mass gravesites, others had been burnt in houses, others were in front of houses, depending on where they met their end and where the people were buried from 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You claim that in the houses you found the skeletons of ten persons; right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, roughly, in the houses that had been burnt down, in the hamlet of Brdjine and Saborsko and so on. They were the bodily remains of the humans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that was about four years after the events that you testified about, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything at all about the circumstances under which these people lost their lives? Were they caught in their houses? Did they -- were they killed by the shells that were falling all around, in the fighting that took place in Saborsko at the time? Do you know anything about the circumstances of their deaths?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what I didn't see, because I was still in captivity. I had been captured. Now, how the people lost their lives is quite evident; they were killed in their houses and set fire to. That can be seen on the thresholds and the hearths. Now, how they were killed I can't say, but yes, there are a hundred witnesses to say how these people were killed. I don't know. Well, they were killed by the JNA and Martic's men, planes, tanks, mortars, the fact that their villages were set fire to, sick, they were ill. That's what I know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you about, what you know. So you don't actually know how those people lost their lives. You are enumerating and giving us multiple options, the variations; the tanks, the mortars, artillery fire, you've listed all that, attacks and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has said he doesn't know, so no point going on about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, have you an answer at all to the question of who killed those people, the bodies of which you found in the villages?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There are hundreds of witnesses, Mr. Milosevic, to tell you how those people lost their lives. I don't want to talk about it because I wasn't there. But what was talked about later on, that's what we heard about so that's what I heard about but don't ask me about things I didn't actually witness, it's just what I learnt later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you, Mr. Vukovic, personally did not see a single person killed, any one of these people, it was just what you learnt of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has never said that he saw anybody killed. He's made the point that he doesn't know himself how they were killed, although he heard. Now, there's no point going on further about that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think there's any point going on further about that either, Mr. May, so I wasn't ask any more questions about that. Thank you. No more questions at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I should like to ask Your Honours to pay attention to paragraph 7, the last few sentences of that paragraph, because I would like to ask the witness to clarify a few points regarding those few sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you said that the attack on Saborsko took place on the 5th of August, 1991. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But here at the end of that second paragraph of your statement, in the B/C/S version, you said as follows: "In the evening of the 5th of August, policemen from Duga Rese left Saborsko, and with them old people, women, and children." Is that right, that the village was left by the elderly women and children that evening of the 5th?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't say that they were not all of them, but never mind. Then you said: "After that, the village was shelled. It would start in the morning and then start again in the evening." Is that right? And this went on for many days, virtually every day.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, you said more houses were damaged, but up until then, no one had been killed or wounded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after the daily shelling in which there were no casualties, as you've said, on the 29th of September, 1991, you were arrested.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you know nothing about what happened in Saborsko after that?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, only there was a great deal of damage; the church and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the period up until you were there, that is the 29th of September. So you don't know that anyone was killed by the shelling in the village?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, you were asked some questions about JNA weapons and fuel depot. Can you tell us where, to your knowledge, that was located?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: This depot is located at the railway station of Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that a Serb area -- or, I'm sorry, was it a Serb area at the time you were there in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was an area that was in those days under the control of the so-called Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to clarify: In 1991 when you were in Saborsko, was that depot under attack by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't have anything to attack with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it blocked by Croatian forces so that the Serbs had no access?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was not blocked?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were asked several questions about certain political events that were occurring in Croatia. Did you interest yourself in those events at the time?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not the events. I was just informed about them, but I didn't have much interest in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about the attack on Saborsko that began on August 5th of 1991. Preceding that attack, were any ultimatums or demands made by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. There weren't any demands or ultimatums. They just blocked the road in Plasko, the road between Licka Jesenica and Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the time of your arrest on September 29th of 1991, are you aware of any demands or ultimatums that were made?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: There weren't any demands or ultimatums made. They were closing themselves in, and they were forming the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Even if somebody wanted to communicate with them, they didn't want to communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, on the 5th of August of 1991, how many men were defending Saborsko, approximately?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, about 50 or 60. All in all, about 50 policemen. About 50 policemen on the 5th of August; those from Duga Rese and those of us from Saborsko. Fifty or 60 policemen, I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And on the 6th of August you said that the policemen from Duga Rese left.

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right, in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When the hundred men came on September 23rd of 1991, did these men offer an effective defence for Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: VLADO VUKOVIC

The witness is a Croat who was 16 years old at the time of the events. He lived in Poljanak in 1991. In August of 1991, three Croats from the area travelling to Saborsko were ambushed and killed. The villagers then decided to form a village guard, which was composed of 25 to 30 men, some armed with hunting rifles. In September of 1991 at an intersection on the road from Vukovici to Poljanak, another two persons were killed. Also in September of 1991, the witness's mother and his sister were captured near Plitvice. His sister spent a month in detention. On the 8th of October, 1991, Vukovici, which is located right next to Poljanak, was shelled by the JNA. The soldiers burned the family house of the witness and when the witness returned, he found that Toma Vukovic had been killed in front of his house and that Kata Matovina was wounded in the upper part of her leg. She had tried to run from the village but was shot. She was 80 to 90 years old, and she later died from her injuries. On the 22nd of October, 1991, Serb soldiers from Plitvice came to Poljanak and arrested three or four civilians and hanged Milan and Ivica Loncar because somebody had taken down a Serbian flag. The sporadic shelling of Poljanak continued. On November 6th of 1991, the witness was with eight other villagers, including his father and some relatives, in a house in Vukovici. He saw somebody running under the window and he went outside and found a group of Serb soldiers standing in the yard, pointing their rifles at him. They yelled at everyone inside the house and ordered them to come out. Everyone obeyed except for one man who was too sick to come out. The Serb soldiers beat and interrogated the men and then lined them up in front of an adjacent house, shot and killed all of them - six men and two women - except for the witness. When the shooting started, the witness jumped over a cellar and mingled amongst the soldiers. One of the soldiers who was called Rambo and who was responsible for killing the men and women said, "No Ustasha should stay alive." However, two other soldiers convinced this Rambo not to kill the witness. Rambo then went to the house and emptied his weapon into the body of the man who had stayed inside the house. When the massacre occurred, 90 to 100 soldiers were in the hamlet. They wore green camouflage uniforms and the commanders had JNA caps with the Red Star. Some of the soldiers wore darker green uniforms than the other soldiers and told the witness that they were part of a JNA special unit from Nis and that they were professional soldiers. They burned everything in the village. The Serb soldiers then went to Poljanak. On the way, they made the witness walk some 20 to 30 metres ahead of the group, apparently because they thought the road might be mined. When they arrived in Poljanak, soldiers forced people who were in the houses to come out, and they separated out the men from the women, lined them up, and killed them. When the witness's mother asked why the Serb soldiers had killed her husband and other men, the soldiers said it was because they were Ustasha. Then the witness and the women remaining in the village were told to leave the village in five seconds or they would be killed.
