utterances.text: So you said then that you had seen 60 people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: About 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, about 60 people, then. Now take a look at paragraph 4 on page 2 of that same statement, line 8, and did you say there: "On the occasion, most of the people," and in brackets it says, "Serbo-Chetniks, I don't know them by name, but most were from the area of Titova Korenica, and I think that were I to see them again, I would recognise them." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now look at the statement you gave on the 15th of September, 1995, the one you gave also to the MUP of Croatia at the police station in Karlovac this time. That is your statement too, isn't it? We're not disputing that, are we? That's right, isn't it, Mr. 1230?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes, without my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But are you challenging that that is your statement at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that you gave this statement also six years before the one you gave to the investigators subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is it correct that on page 1, paragraph 3 of that statement, the one I've just drawn your attention to, that you said the following: "On that day when I was captured together with the other occupants of the house, since I was inside the house, I saw through the window that something was happening in front of the house. To be precise, I saw some people move in front of the house, and I went outside to see who was out there, and I was captured then by Serb soldiers/Chetniks." And then there's another sentence after that which reads as follows: "They were all local men from the surrounding areas." Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1230. Let us go back now to your statement given to the investigators on the 27th and 28th of February, 2001. Please look at paragraph 17 of that statement, line 7. Tell me, is it true that it says there that, ten years after the event you describe, you said: "The soldiers told me that they were a special JNA unit from Nis and that they were professional soldiers. I felt that they were professional soldiers by the military terms they used. This special unit was wearing a camouflage uniform in a darker green colour than the uniforms worn by the other soldiers in the village." Is that what it says in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes, in paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time you were giving this statement to the investigators, therefore, I had already been abducted and brought to The Hague. You certainly know that. That is, on the 28th of February, 2001. My question is the following: When did you learn that you would appear as a witness in the case against me before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you just answer that again, please, so the interpreters can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A week or two ago. I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in which of the three previously given statements - one given eight, the other six years before this one - given to the investigators, you mention professional soldiers of the JNA, that is, a special unit from Nis. Please look at all those statements and answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take it that there is no reference in these statements, but you put to the witness that when he made the statement to the investigators in February 2001 that you had already been brought to The Hague. That wasn't so, because you didn't arrive until July, if my recollection is right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I meant -- I meant that the indictment had already been issued long since, prior to that date. Maybe I misspoke. You're quite right as far as the date is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're right about this particular indictment. The Kosovo indictment, of course, had been issued but not, as I recollect, the Croatia one. But in any event, yes, what do you want to put to the witness next? There's no mention of the Nis special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it beyond dispute, Mr. 1230, that in all three previously given statements you explicitly claimed that all the soldiers who were present at the event you're testifying about were local people and that you would be able to recognise most of them? Is that beyond dispute?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: I assumed so, but I didn't know them by name, and I could recognise them by their faces, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm drawing your attention once again to this sentence in statement which we can call number 3. It is the 15th of September, 1995, in which you say they were all local people from the surroundings. That is what you said in all these three previous statements, the one given to the Centre for Human Rights and two to the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that mischaracterises what's in the statements. It does say that in that statement, but I don't believe it says they're all locals in the other statements. It says most of them are locals but it's different in all different statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can no doubt re-examine about them. I suppose the point is this, Witness 1230: You did not mention the special unit from Nis in the earlier statements. Now, I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, but that seems to be the position. Why did you not mention that unit in the earlier statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only mentioned the things they spoke about amongst themselves later. No one ever asked me what they were talking about amongst themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, I see. I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since I hope this is unambiguous, the fact that you said that they were all locals from the surroundings, you made a statement about everything you knew at the time, and you say what you know in a time period that was closer to the events than the later ones. Now, tell me, looking at these three statements and comparing them with what you say in the statement given to the investigators, is it beyond dispute that the number of soldiers present at the event you are testifying about kept increasing, kept growing as time went by?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now look, please, in your statement number 1 that I referred to first. You said in paragraph 3 there were ten or so Chetniks in camouflage uniforms in front of the house. So about ten. Then in the second one, you said 20 plus 40. So it's more than doubled; quadrupled, in fact. And then in the statement to the investigators ten years later, in paragraph 17 you say 90 -- between 90 and 100. So from the time of your first statement when you say you saw about ten, and then in all three statements you say they were locals that you knew, then you reach the figure of as many as 100, and only in this last statement do you say that they were JNA soldiers, and you even go on to specify that they came from a Nis garrison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: There were ten of them around the house when I went out, but I couldn't count them. I didn't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say when you went out you saw about ten. And then in your second statement, you say 20 who entered and ordered you to go out of the house and then you saw another 40 outside. And in the first you say that you went out -- when you went out, you saw about ten; and in the second, that 20 of them came in and told you to come out, and when you went out you saw another 40. Are you disputing that or not, Mr. 1230?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: I saw the others when I came out, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But in your first statement, that's what you say; when you went out, you saw about ten Chetniks. Very well, Mr. 1230. I sincerely regret all the things that happened to your family and the fact that you were so young at the time and witnessed all this. Please explain, how did these rather large changes occur in your statements with respect to the description of the men there, their number, and the description of the event itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He has explained about the unit. I think he's answered, really, about the numbers. Is there anything you want to add to your previous answer in relation to the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In those days -- at the time, I was unable to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You could not count when you gave the first statement or the second or the third. It appears that you were able to assume the number when you were giving your statement to the investigators. Is that right, Mr. 1230?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: The number is unspecified. It's a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that in -- not in any of the previous three statements that you gave to various bodies, that nowhere is mention made of soldiers of the JNA, especially not from Nis as the perpetrators of the crime you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think he's dealt with that. He's explained how the Nis unit came to be referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the explanation, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He said he wasn't asked about what they were talking about. Now, he's given his explanation. We shall have to consider it. We can't go on going over the same point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that as members of that unit, in your statements you describe those members as being local inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've made your point. We see the discrepancy. He has given his explanation. We will have to consider it. We cannot go on going over the same point.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I didn't convey what I wanted. I just referred to what he said, and he literally said that they were all local people from the surroundings. It's not a matter of what I want; I just read the statements that I was given by the side opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. 1230, is it undisputed that in several places you identify as the only direct perpetrator a certain Rambo who was also a local inhabitant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: That was just the nickname of that person. Now, whether he was a local, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But from the descriptions you gave, I gathered that you were able to identify that person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes, by his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Finally, in paragraph 2 of your statement, you say that after Easter in 1991, the JNA occupied the Plitvice Lakes. Isn't that so, Mr. 1230?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, where did you get this information from that the JNA had occupied Plitvice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: I lived at Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I can gather that you are claiming that you saw with your own eyes that the JNA had occupied Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: I saw their tanks and troops on our roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer the following question: Did anyone advise you to include in your fourth statement, the one given to the investigators, to mention this special unit from Nis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone make any suggestions to you in connection with this alleged occupation by the JNA of the Plitvice Lakes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you have any explanation for such considerable discrepancies between these four statements of yours, the previous three and this fourth one that you gave to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: This was a more detailed one and more questions were asked about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. 1230. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I would like to ask the witness to explain to us a few more points

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although I know this must be for you very hard in view of everything you lived through, but I would like to ask you if you could explain to Their Honours, in view of these several statements that you gave, in the first one in sequence following the event, you were explicit in saying that the person who killed those people on the spot where you were was someone who used to work at the station in Korenica, and you did not mention the name Rambo at all. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: He was the commander, the one who was working in Korenica, and Rambo was the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in your statement to the investigators, you said that the person shooting was Rambo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But in your first statement you said it was a large man who used to work in the police station in Korenica and that he executed those people. This is the first statement that you gave in the centre in Zagreb. It is on page 1, towards the end of the page. Please look.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: There was chaos because one started shooting, but it doesn't say that the commander was shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But it says here, "The one who killed all of them noticed me and came to kill me too." That's what you stated then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes, but it doesn't say that it was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The commander. But you didn't mention Rambo at all. You mentioned this heavy man who killed everyone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: No. He was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And why didn't you say then that it was Rambo who was the perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Obviously no one asked me about that on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look at the other statements, the one of the 21st of June and the other one of the 15th of September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to tire you. You will be able to read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, you use the plural. You say that all those who were in front of the house started shooting at you. Look at the second page of the statement of the 21st of June, paragraph 3. "Then they started shooting at us." You don't mention Rambo again anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic, we have the point. He mentions Rambo first on the -- in the statement of the 15th of September. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He doesn't mention Rambo, Your Honours, in the statement of the 15th of September either. So will you please take note of the fact that each time the execution is described in a completely different manner. You have all the statements, I don't need to dwell on it, I'm just asking you to take note of that when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He refers to Rambo on the 15th of September statement. "I heard them refer to each other by nicknames such as Rambo. Rambo was their ringleader."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite precise and for me to make myself quite clear, in the statement of the 15th of September, he mentions Rambo but only as a man who bragged having killed many Croats. And you'll find that in the statement. In that third statement, he mentions him as bragging of having killed many Croats but he doesn't say that he was the perpetrator of the execution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, you've been asked many questions about prior interviews that you gave, and just to be clear, from the documents it appears there were three prior interviews; one dated 16 April 1993, 21 June 1995, and 15 September 1995. Can you tell the Court, just in brief terms, the circumstances of these interviews, how long they lasted, for example. You can take them one at a time, if you wish. For example, the one on 16 April 1993, do you recall how long that interview was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly how long it could have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Well, it depended. Sometimes half an hour, sometimes an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did any of these interviews, the three that have been referred to, last for more than an hour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you say anything about what the focus of the interviews was? Was it focused on perpetrators who were in the area or what was the focus of the interviews?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Mostly about the people killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were you asked in detail about all of the soldiers who were present at the event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You state in your statement that was given to the ICTY that you saw that the three commanders had JNA caps in their belts. Do you recollect that? That's in paragraph 17.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court in your own words how it is that you came to learn that there was a Nis special unit present. What was it that allowed you to learn that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: After the execution, when they'd shot everybody and when the bomb was thrown, we were taken a little further away from the house and the soldiers talked amongst themselves there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you hear that allowed you to learn that they were from Nis, that they were a special unit from Nis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: They spoke about weapons. They spoke about the place where they had been before that. They spoke about the attack, they spoke about -- talked amongst themselves and mentioned Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And were you -- in your prior interviews, were you asked questions about this, about conversations that were held among the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to -- well, let me ask you this: When you and the others were brought out of the house, were -- were -- you say in your statement that soldiers were shouting and were beating the men as they came out of the house. Do you remember that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it -- was it just one soldier doing that or more than one soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: There were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 12 that soldiers - and it's in the plural - started shooting, but you also say that you think that one soldier is responsible for the killing. Do you see that in paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there just one soldier shooting or was there more than one soldier shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: More than one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what made you think that one -- if there was more than one soldier shooting, what made you think that one soldier was responsible for the killing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Because many were shooting around the houses, around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So from what you could observe, it appeared to you that one soldier was actually hitting the people but others were shooting. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Yes, that they were shooting towards me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you repeat the answer, please. You're asked by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But I wasn't in a situation to be able to see that, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, I would ask you to have the clock in mind. We need to get through another witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have just one or two more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were asked lots of questions about how many soldiers were present, and in the first statement it says in the statement, the April 16, 1993, statement, that you saw ten soldiers in front of the house. Were those the only soldiers who were present in the village or were there others also present in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: There were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And as you sit here today, what's your best recollection of how many soldiers were present not just around the house but in the entire village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: Around the house, about -- I can't say exactly, but 20 or 30, perhaps more. There was a larger group. But I was also in a situation in which they were questioning me, so I couldn't really look around. And then there was another group in the village that was setting fire to the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So all in all, taking all the soldiers in the village, can you give us an estimate today of what your best recollection is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1230
utterances.text: It can just be an assumption, an opinion. I couldn't see them all; guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1230, thank you for coming to the Tribunal. That concludes your evidence. You are now free to go. Just wait for the blinds. We'll give the statements that were produced by the accused the next Defence number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, those obviously have to be under seal because they have the witness's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Defence Exhibit 156, Your Honour, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, while that witness is leaving, before we have the next witness, we will deal with the matters concerning the Rule 92 bis statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The first witness is the Witness C-1162, Jasna Mihajlovic, and she deals with Eastern Slavonia, Erdut, the killing in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you'd like to -- I was going to say you could produce that. We don't seem to have an usher. If someone would assist, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And maybe one additional remark as to this witness; the witness has meanwhile a different name, and it can be seen from the first page. She has now a different last name, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll take an exhibit number for this one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 481, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next witness is C-1089, Stjepan Dasovic, and he relates also to Eastern Slavonia, to Klisa.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 482.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next one is Mario Curic. He has the number C-1088, and it relates to Dubrovnik, and here in particular the town of Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 483.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the last one, finally, C-1127, Djelo Jusic. He is again a Dubrovnik witness dealing with the festival hall and the attacks on hotels. And that would be it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 484.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as -- may I ask what happened to the 92 bis witness? I didn't quite understand. They're not in -- on the schedule here. Have we got their statements for the first time now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They've been admitted without cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Ma'am, you've been granted certain protective measures by the Trial Chamber, so during your testimony we will refer to you by your pseudonym, C-1126.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we just break for two minutes, please, just to check the voice distortion. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask if a piece of paper could be put in front of you and ask you to take a look at that and tell me just by your answer yes or no whether that's your name on the first line of that document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: It is there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Now, to further protect your identity, you will see at the bottom of this sheet a list of names of people and places, and with the Chamber's permission, we will ask you to refer to those names during your testimony. So if at any time you need to refer to any of these names or to the place listed at the bottom, if you could just use the substitute on this list, the Trial Chamber will know what name you're referring to. Can you do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this sheet we've listed the village that the witness comes from simply as "the village," which is how she will be referring to it during her testimony. You will find this village in the atlas Exhibit 336 on page 23, and the coordinates for the village are E-2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, in recent days did you have a chance to go over your witness statement in the presence of an officer of the court and attest to its accuracy, subject to corrections which were noted, and then did you sign that documentation showing that you had attested your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, my understanding --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- is that you have to turn off your microphone while the witness is answering with the voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, we would just like to make a moment to correct one error in the statement. If I could ask that a copy of the witness's statement in her own language could be put in front of her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And ask you please to turn to paragraph 7 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: In reviewing your statement after it was signed, did you become aware that there was an error in one of the dates in the paragraph in the version of the statement in your own language that you signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And what was that error and what should the correct date be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: The correct date should read the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And what date is listed in the B/C/S version of the statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: In the statement, it says the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to point out to the Court that this is apparently a translation error from the English version of the statement to the B/C/S. The date is correct as 1991 in the version of the statement that was read to the witness and which she signed in 1996 but was incorrect in the B/C/S version of the statement that she signed earlier this month. And subject to this correction, I would like to offer the statement of C-1126 into evidence under Rule 92 bis, under seal as a protected witness. We have also prepared a redacted version of this statement which can be made publicly available.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, Prosecution Exhibit 485.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can make the following summary of the witness's statement: This witness is a Croat woman who was 31 at the time of the events in question. She lived in Vukovar until the 22nd of August, 1991, and on that date she and her husband went to visit her mother in a village just south of Vukovar. She couldn't get back to Vukovar because it was completely surrounded by the JNA and so the witness lived in this village until 20 January, 1992. After the ZNG members left this village in September, the residents were very scared because of what was going on in the villages around them and because of the stories that they heard from the refugees who passed through the village. On 13 October, 1991, there were negotiations with the JNA about the surrender of the village and the JNA issued an ultimatum. People in the town were very afraid since Tovarnik and Lovas had already been taken, and the witness heard from people coming from those towns that Croatians there had been slaughtered and their houses had been burned. The JNA entered the town the following morning. After homes were searched, people had to put a piece of white textile on the gate of the fence of the house. Croatian residents were also ordered to wear white ribbons on their left arm. No one could leave the village since it was surrounded and there were checkpoints with guards at each exit. During the search after the village was taken over, they found rifles at the homes of some of the Croats, and the Croats who had the rifles were almost killed for that. In contrast, Serbs who had weapons were simply asked to present the weapon for listing it down and then got it back. A kind of census was arranged in the local community building. After the census, about 30 non-Serbs from the village were arrested. Many of them were beaten, and approximately ten were expelled from the village with their families. On one day, the witness was ordered to tidy up the village guest house, and there she heard from a soldier that other soldiers were fighting each other about who was going to be given the job and the privilege of slaughtering the priest from Tovarnik. The witness will testify that her husband was taken for questioning in November. The witness herself was ordered to come for questioning at 9.00 that morning. She was questioned by two guards and told to go home and come back at 5.00 p.m. that afternoon. The witness was questioned again the next day with her husband. She was taken into a room in which was a Hungarian person already, and that person she saw beaten and hit on his face. The witness was threatened and grabbed by the throat. After that, the witness and her husband had to report each morning to the local community building, and both had to go for forced labour, as well as other Croatians. For example, the witness on one occasion had to load corn into storage outside at 10 below zero. Later on, another group of the army replaced the previous one in the village. The witness and her husband were helped by the military police to flee the village. They learned that they were on a list to be taken to Vukovar, and they were told that if they had gone to Vukovar, they were supposed to be killed. Your Honours, I would note also that there are two additional sections of her statement mentioned in paragraphs 7 and 9 of the proofing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. summary that I have not read out, and I would ask that if the subjects of those paragraphs are discussed during her testimony, that they could be covered in private session. And I have two just additional matters that came up during her proofing session, listed in the proofing summary as paragraphs 14 and 15, and I would ask if we could go into private session for just a moment so that I could cover those questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the two points mentioned by Mr. McKeon, 14 and 15, as to be discussed in private session, I see nothing in paragraphs 14 and 15 that is linked to this. Perhaps they were some other numbers, other paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Paragraphs 14 and 15 of the summary. You should have a copy of it attached to the bundle you were given.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. I was looking at the paragraphs in the statement. That explains it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll have cross-examination after the adjournment. We will adjourn now for twenty minutes. Witness C-1126, we're going to adjourn now for 20 minutes. During the adjournment, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. We will adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1126, if there are any matters which you would prefer to answer in private session when you're asked questions, just say so and we can go into private session to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Madam 1126, I am not going to ask you any questions linked to the violence you were exposed to because I do not wish to hurt you by asking any unpleasant questions, but I do wish to establish certain circumstances and particularly the identity of the persons referred to. So my questions will be limited to that alone. In paragraphs 19 and 20, you described the circumstances under which these things happened to you, this abuse that you are referring to, by a person that you describe as a short man who was wearing a dirty uniform, with a broken nose. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In order to establish his identity, if possible, will you please tell me, what did his uniform look like, the one he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: He was wearing an olive-grey uniform, SMB uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, this SMB colour, that's the regular military uniform, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Of the Yugoslav People's Army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As in paragraph 16, towards the end, let me just quote you: "I saw how the Serbs from the village, those who did not join the others in the beginning, were given JNA uniforms and put them on." So those were the same uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, did you notice whether there were any insignia on the uniform so that one might, on the basis of those insignia, possibly establish the formation that person belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: On the cap there was a five-cornered star.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was a regular uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did this man say anything about himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were you able to assume by his speech where that person came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: He said himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I think that he said he was from the surroundings of Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps have any information as to who his superior was, if he had any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know nothing about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that he was wearing that uniform, and also as we see that the uniform was distributed to everyone, did you have the impression that that person was a JNA member or perhaps someone from some other unit that was using those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: They came in groups. This soldier came with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But I assume you know that in those days, virtually every household in the then-Yugoslavia that had a military conscript had a JNA uniform.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: For the reserve, for the reserve forces. So you know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, then I won't ask you anything more about it. In paragraphs 23 and onwards, you mention a certain person whose name is also protected here. On the list of protected names he is mentioned as Person E,

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of whom you say that he was from Sid; is that right? And who, according to what can be read from your statement, behaved bestially and engaged in abuse, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did he say he was from Sid or did you hear it from someone or, rather, how did you know that he came from Sid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I heard that from Person D, that he used to live in the environs of Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From Person D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I heard from Person D that Person E lived in the environs of Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, do you know whether he belonged to any paramilitary unit or something that might have been called a volunteer unit or something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I am unable to answer that. I only know that he wore a uniform with the cap worn by generals or something like that. He appeared to be something like a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A kind of general's cap, you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does that cap look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Like the police, but it wasn't the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What colour was the cap?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I think it was also the same colour as the uniform, SMB.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did he have any insignias?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: On his shoulders he did have some insignias, but I was unable to recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, in paragraph 31, you say that a group of those men among whom were these two who abused you was replaced by another group of soldiers, reservists, and members of the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: The military police, yes. Now, whether they were reservists, I can't say, I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But am I mistaken if I say that these were members, judging by what one can conclude from this, were reserve forces of the JNA and the military police of the JNA? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, Madam C-1126, it is also true that these people, this group that came after this first group, were attentive in relation to you and your family? They protected you from any kind of mistreatment, that a certain local Serb tried to inflict upon you, a person who is marked on the list of names as Person A?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that both the man in the dirty uniform and this second one that we mentioned after that as Person E who were in the previous group, they differed from this second group. So were they members of some paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Person A remained in the village until the end. However, Person B, that was first to abuse me, had already left in the direction of Vukovar. After Person B, Person E arrived, who also abused me, and I told him that Person B had harassed me and mistreated me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But when this group of reservists of the JNA and the military police came, they protected you, and after that, no one could abuse you any longer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: These three persons that I mentioned were not there at the same time. They were not in the village at the same time. They came in different time periods. And after all of them, this group of people arrived who helped me in a sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but as far as I'm able to gather, Person A was present in the village while these persons were there, and they protected you from this person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: They only protected me from Person A, whereas Persons B and E had already left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they'd left the village. There was no need to protect you from them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: In those days, no one knew whether they would come back or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a few points regarding some more general matters. First of all, tell me, please, until August you lived with your husband in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, until August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 5, you say that already in August there was shooting and shelling due to which you actually left Vukovar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No. That was not the reason that we left Vukovar, but my mother was sick, and we went to see her in the village to help her in her work. However, we didn't know that there was so many checkpoints everywhere, and it was very difficult to move around. So we were unable to go back to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it follows that Vukovar, when you left it, was already surrounded; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: It was surrounded but not totally. It was still possible to move around, but movement was restricted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you passed through certain checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes. Both I and my husband, we left to help my mother for a day, to do a certain job, and after that we simply couldn't get back, because within the space of 24 hours, everything was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you and your husband left Vukovar without any difficulty and no one prevented you from doing that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: They did question us, asking us where we were going and why we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone mistreat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No, not on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in Vukovar when you were leaving it, were there any members of the National Guards Corps, and how many of them at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I'm unable to answer that question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Had some fighting already started in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: One could hear shots in the streets, shooting from a distance and shells going off. There were tanks going from Vukovar towards Borovo Selo and back on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge as to who was fighting who over there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I didn't see who was fighting who, but I did see freight vehicles and tanks going towards Borovo Selo and coming back. Barrels were pointed at the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In those days before you left Vukovar, did you have any knowledge to the effect that many others, both Serbs and Croats and members of other ethnicities, were also leaving Vukovar or fleeing Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I have no knowledge that they were fleeing. Some people went to visit people, but no one was fleeing. No one felt that anything bad was about to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So in those days, as far as you knew, at least on the basis of your own knowledge, there were no killings over there, no crimes due to which people were leaving Vukovar and seeking shelter in Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how far is your home or apartment or house you lived in, how far is it from the Vukovar barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I'm unable to give you the exact number of kilometres, but it is about halfway between the barracks and Borovo Selo. Halfway, midway between those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Roughly how far is that? I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, about six kilometres. Five kilometres. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear or learn anything about fire being opened from the city centre against the barracks in Vukovar and vice versa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You know nothing. But did you have any knowledge of water, electricity shortages, and the blockade of the barracks in Vukovar and the blockade of the people who were inside? Did you hear anything about that while you were still able to obtain information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn anything about the blockade of the barracks in Vukovar, the fact that water, electricity supplies were cut off, food deliveries were not permitted, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In paragraph 6 of your statement, you say that the village -- Mr. McKeon, I think he said when mentioning the village that we should use the word "village" for it -- that this was a village with about 600 inhabitants of different ethnicities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 7, already in the first sentence you say that when you arrived to the village, Serb women with children as well as young Serb men had already left the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes. They were not in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we can't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the interpreters didn't hear the question. Perhaps you could repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the witness whether she knew anything about the reasons that had prompted Serb women, young men, and children to leave the village, and the answer I was given is that the witness knows nothing about that. Is everything all right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that in the village at that time there was a formation of the Croatian National Guards Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes. That was in September 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that to all intents and purposes, the village had been taken over by the Croatian National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No. It wasn't taken over because the guard was in Ilok at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I drew that conclusion, so I would like to check it out. Could you explain that to me? Because in paragraph 8 of your statement, you say that: "At the time we arrived in the village, there were already members of the National Guards Unit there. Some 30 of them were staying in the village cultural centre," and so on. I don't want to read any further. So how many of them in total were there in the village when you arrived? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, I think there must have been about 20 or 30 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just establish the situation in the village when you arrived. In view of the quotation I read out a moment ago and what we took note of a moment ago. Serbs, women with children, and Serb young men, they were not in the village. And in the village, who was present were the members of the Croatian National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes. But there were also Serbs who remained in the village. However, nobody touched them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I understand that. I'm just trying to establish whether there was a cause-and-effect relationship, which seems to me to be obvious, between the fact that the National Guards Corps was there and that these people left the village. You then go on to say here that they would be replaced every two weeks, and I'm quoting what you say. I think you said two weeks or something like that. And then you say they were only armed with infantry weapons, and in September they withdrew to Ilok. How come you know they only had infantry weapons on them; and in general terms, how are you able to conclude and specify as to the type of weapons they actually had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: They actually only had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me this: How many shifts did you notice? Because you said that they -- one group would replace another group several times.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I think there was a mistake here when it said that they were changed every two weeks. Perhaps there was an error in the translation. There was actually just one group, and they stayed there for a couple of days or a week and then they withdrew to Ilok, so that there was no replacement or changing over every two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say it's an error in the translation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes. That's a mistake. The other armies that came in, the JNA and the Territorial Defence units, they would rotate every two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as I was able to understand you, you say that your husband was involved militarily in these village watches, village guards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes. He only stood guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was he? What did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, he had a rifle that was not working. He didn't have any ammunition or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, as in paragraph 12 you say that JNA planes rocketed the village and hit some sort of borders or barriers and the cultural centre but that nothing else was damaged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, when the ZNGs withdrew, the ZNG members withdrew before the army entered the village, the village was left on its own, unprotected, and I assume that the people were afraid. I don't know why they set up those things there, but as soon as they put the sandbags up, an hour later the planes turned up and rocketed the defences, these sandbags.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: But nobody was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody was killed and nothing was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: There wasn't any major material damage, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the ZNG members were no longer there. They had already left the area; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So before that, they used these sandbags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, the villagers, the people who stayed on in the village, placed these sandbags at their own initiative. And just as they had set them up, an hour later the planes turned up and started targeting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. I understand. Now, in paragraph 13, you say that the JNA quickly, after the agreement reached with the leaders of the village, entered the village and they searched the houses because they were looking for weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They entered every house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then already in paragraph 14, you say that you know that they did not mistreat anybody. Is that what you said? That nobody was mistreated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, after they had made a list of all the inhabitants, then they shut them up, that same day in the afternoon when the army entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is the point I wish to clarify: In paragraph 14, it says: "The following morning, the JNA was on time..." because prior to that, you say who was there, the negotiations, how the negotiations evolved, and things like that, and you said that the result was that the JNA would enter the village without a fight and that all weapons were to be surrendered to the soldiers straight away and that searches would be conducted of all the houses. That was what was agreed upon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 14, you say: "The following morning, the JNA was punctual and at 0900 hours it entered the village. The infantry entered first, followed by the tanks."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Serbs who had left the village before and whose names I had mentioned earlier on, and so on and so forth, that's not important. Let me just find the sentence I wish to highlight. It's the next sentence, in fact, and it says the following: "The soldiers entered the houses and searched them all, and then the next sentence is: "As far as I know, they did not maltreat anybody then." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, just while they were searching the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 10, the last sentence there, you said that the Croatian mothers with their children left the village before the JNA entered it and that there was some young men who had weapons in their possession too; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, in paragraph 8, you said that the village guards or village watch was equipped exclusively with hunting weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't follow. I don't understand this. Why did these young Croats leave the village when you say that there was no weaponry in it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that these ZNGs had left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And was there any other purpose for the JNA's entry and for them searching the houses except for the fact that they were looking for weapons? And you said that they didn't mistreat anyone while they were doing so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: While they were searching the houses, they didn't touch anybody, no, while this search process was going on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, you say in paragraph 16 that after the searches had been conducted, the men fared worse, that is to say the men in whose houses they did find rifles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what happened to those men? Mr. McKeon used the term -- I think he said they almost killed them. I don't know that this -- I can't explain that expression "almost killed them," so could you explain it to me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Once the houses had been searched, all of us who happened to be in the village had to go to the local commune with our ID cards for them to make a list of the population and inhabitants who were in the village at the time. After that, those people who were -- whom the JNA found -- whom the JNA found reason to detain in that same cultural centre - I don't know why - they were detained there for a few days, maybe as much as eight days, whereas others were taken off with their families from the village, and we knew nothing about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, was anybody killed at all at that -- on that occasion in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: A gentleman was killed who was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how did he meet his end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: As far as I know, they took him away towards the road leading to Vukovar, and his hands were tied with a wire, and they shot him in the back. And they wanted to make it appear as if he was trying to run, to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that from someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear that from someone, but they put the body on a tractor trailer, and he was left lying there for a day until they finally buried him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So who drove the tractor with the trailer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it one of the villagers who found him there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: None of the locals found him. It was the people who killed him, they brought him back. And they said that he was trying to escape. He was captured and that they had to shoot him in his attempt to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So that's the explanation they gave; they said they were forced to shoot because he tried to escape. Now, tell me this, then, please -- and you said that the men in whose houses rifles were found fared worst. What kind of rifles were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were ordinary hunting rifles, because there were a lot of hunters in the village, lots of people who liked hunting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So do you then claim that there were no automatic weapons or any military equipment that was found?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. All I do know is that the people who were found in possession of weapons had licenses to carry those hunting rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. There are a lot of hunters. Now, does the name Tomislav Mercep ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this man precisely at the time that was a forerunner to these events that you're testifying about, he distributed weapons, first of all automatic rifles, to the surrounding villages, including this particular village, the one you're testifying about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you have any knowledge at all as to the activities of the Tomislav Mercep formations and similar units in the area, anything that might have reached your ears, any piece of information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So all you know about those formations was what you knew through the members, several tens of members of the National Guards Corps that left the village before the JNA entered, that was the only formation you saw and that you know about at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I understood your testimony, they did not commit any violence in the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: You mean the Croatian National Guards Corps? No, they didn't mistreat anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't take anybody away with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Just very few follow-up questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Ma'am, there was some questioning about the uniform of one particular man. Could you tell us, just in general terms, what sort of uniforms were worn by the people that were in your village, and if you could tell from those uniforms whether they were regular JNA members, reservists, Territorial Defence, paramilitary, or perhaps something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, I recognised the uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army, and some of the soldiers who were there were wearing camouflage uniforms. They were very untidy looking, had long beards. They were all dusty. They even smelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And the soldiers that were in your village, did it appear to you that they were all working together at a single purpose or were they doing something else and each going off and doing their own thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I had the feeling that they were all working for a single purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: All right. And again you were asked some questions about this man in the regular military uniform and the patches on his uniform, so on and so forth. Did you learn from him what he was doing with the military after he left your village? In other words, where he was going.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about Person E. Did you learn at some point what his official duty was in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, he was the chief of some kind of police of theirs, and he had a group of men he issued orders to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Did he have any responsibilities in the area of interrogating and questioning residents of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And you said he appeared to be some sort of a policeman. Would that have been, from the uniform, in your view --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: -- a military police or a civilian policeman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, he had the cap on like a general's cap or a police cap, and he had an olive-green uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Was that the same uniform that was worn by the JNA that was in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, similar except for the cap. All the rest was similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about Person A, and I think in the midst of one of the questions he was referred to in the question as a local Serb. Was Person A from your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No, Person A was another village also in the surrounding area of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about the weaponry of the guards, and you gave the answer that your husband had a rifle that was not working and had no ammunition. Let me ask you first of all, were you also involved in these local guards as well as your husband?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Do you have any jobs or responsibilities with the local guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And what were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, as a woman, I was told to come to their assistance if anybody happened to be wounded or anything bad happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that your husband had a rifle that was not working and had no ammunition. Was this unusual that the members of the guards had non-working weapons or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: It was usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: And in your dealings with the local guards, did you ever see any automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Finally, you were asked some questions about the people in the village who were found, Croats who were found with rifles. I think in your statement you said that you heard that they fared worst amongst the people that were beaten. Could you tell us what you heard happened to those people who were found with rifles or weapons. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, they were interrogated and they were beaten a lot. And afterwards, they were escorted further on, taken away. As far as I know, they were taken to Serbia, to some prisons there while their families were put into a truck and driven off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: In your statement, you referred to ten people and their families who were forced to leave the village. Would that be amongst those people who were found with weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-1126
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: That's all I have, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness C-1126, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you are now free to go. If you would just wait while the blinds are brought down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn until next Tuesday morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could, I wanted to inform the court that a witness order list will be distributed by the Prosecution to all parties sometime tomorrow, for next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If there are any changes, the earlier it's distributed, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The legal officer, please. We will adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of July, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.23 p.m.,
